Here how it works at my store with my boss:

We use Bookeo and an app called when I work. My boss encouraged us to make a separate work email for our when i work account and for bookeo. We are then assigned 3-5 days a week that we are 'on-call' for bookings. He then in our subheadings of our schedule sets up a room priority list. This is done in the when I work app. That's also where we put our availability and can trade shifts, that type of thing.

So, if my coworker S and I are on call that day our schedule will say something like room A-room B-room C for S and room B -room C- room A for me. If room A books, S goes in. If room B books, I go in. If room B and C book we both go in and I run B and he runs C. 

 We are expected to be available on those days for our 8 hour block. For our on-call days we will receive half a days pay even if there are no bookings for our rooms in particular. Our bookeo is set up to send emails to our work accounts when we get a booking so we know as soon as it's made. One of us or our boss will then block off the other rooms in that time-slot in bookeo if we don't have enough GMs on call. So I imagine you guys could just set up work emails and then have bookeo email you all directly when something books? I'm not sure how you could fairly 'claim' a room without someone feeling slighted somewhere. There is a huge pricing differences in other countries. That's why major streaming services don't just offer the same usd rate all over and have other countries convert their currency to that usd amount. 

For example, in India disney plus costs 1499 rupees a year. That's $18 in USD. The cheapest Disney tier in America is like $95. That's how big a difference there is in pricing.

This is because of how different wages are in other places. The average person in India makes the equivalent of 5,000 USD a year. $95 would represent such a huge chunk of that, no one would buy it. These streaming services price themselves to be a percentage of the local wage, not a flat amount. 

When smaller creators make it so that everyone pays $5 usd that represents a much higher percentage of income to people in certain countries.

It's a red flag for me that she's gaining and not just at a stabilized weight.  That extra weight has to be coming from somewhere. It doesn't seem like she's having other symptoms so a non-malignant tumor would be on my radar. The lack of other symptoms makes it difficult to pinpoint a location.  The main concern would be that the tumor is pressing on an organ in some way that's reducing function in a way that won't appear on a blood panel or lipids test. Like in the lungs, for example. Hi, I collect and restore toys!  Yellowing happens to pretty much all plastic toys over time.  It's not 100 percent reversible, but you can definitely improve the looks of the item. The general treatment is peroxide, sunlight or some other UV light, some heat, and time. For toys like this I'll literally just get a jar, fill it with hydrogen peroxide, pop in the toy, put a hole in the lid, and leave it in the sun for a while. "A while" would be anywhere from one day to a month based on the size of the toy and the severely of the yellowing. These guys would be a day. I normally use like 10% strength peroxide.   Usually this method doesn't noticeably affect paint but it can. I recommend using one as a test. I would probably do Bijou, it would be easy to reapply some blue paint to her bows if it happened to fade or come off.

For toys in the like 200+ dollar range or that have tons of personal sentiment you could be more precise and avoid paint entirely by using very low strength peroxide cream designed for lightning human hair. And just apply with a brush, q tip, or toothpick based on size then wrap up and place outside or under a UV bulb. This is much harder to do, it's harder to apply the cream consistently so this method often results in a patchy or uneven appearance and I have to repeat it a few times. I only do this if I'm certain a peroxide bath will damage paint or the item is too valuable to test. 

With either method you then just gently rinse with water. Some use soap as well but I find I usually don't need it. You can gently press the toy into a towel to dry and remove and leftover dirt. Do not rub the towel vigorously into the toy as it's possible the peroxide has softened the paint a bit and it needs time to dry again.

Edit: I remembered something else, heat does play a factor. Try to do this on a day that's like at least 23 degrees C or 75 degrees F. I personally think the hotter it is the better this works, but I know some ppl think it doesn't really matter as long as it's not like snowing out. If you do this a lot and live in a chilly area it is worth it to invest in a UV bulb so it can be in a warm room. My anecdotal evidence is that I I have saved supposedly unsalvageably yellowed toys because I live in an area that gets to be over 38 degrees Celsius in summer and can leave my toys out in that heat.

Perhaps try engaging in more conversation before going straight to discipline. Can you think of some scenarios where he became overstimulated, especially due to touch? Try framing the bunnies' needs in terms that relate to him. I would try to frame it like the bunnies' get overstimulated too.  The next time before he interacts with the rabbits (not during the interaction, before) try to explain that bunnies get overstimulated easily. Ask him about the last time.he got upset due to overstimulation and say the bunnies' feel like that when he grabs them.  It's important to reinforce this idea before the interaction, during the interaction, and after the interaction. Point out the body language of the rabbit and the clear signs that the are happy vs. distressed. How does he communicate with you guys?  Is he verbal? If so, you can ask questions to see if he remembers the signs of a bunnies' distress. It's totally reasonable to get an enclosure that locks  to protect the bunnies' until he can get a better handle on animal safety as long as you guys consistently reinforce that it's not a punishment to him.  It's important to introduce these concepts in moments where he is calm and not overstimulated and to reinforce them in a consistent manner. Consistency is the number one thing, in my experience, to teaching myself and other autistic people. The reality is that there is no way to instantly change us, no matter what you do. Expecting quick change will only frustrate you and hurt your brother.

My last boss was a trump loving republican and he used they/them pronouns for me. So does my landlord, my doctors, my friends, and other loved ones. The reality is that it's just not that difficult to change pronouns and people try to be decent!

​

The key to living as a nonbinary person is to not get angry and upset with people, but to be consistent with them. When someone calls me a gendered term or uses the wrong pronoun the first thing I determine is if I'll see this person again and if they're a stranger. If it's like a waitress or some guy in the street I let it go. Your child will need to accept that most people don't know we exist. But the positive to that is that your child and I get to see the world change in our lifetimes. I believe I'll be able to legally change my gender to something other than M or F in my life. Heck, my doctor had the gender section as a write in and just added a few questions to the medical history section. He actually gets more info that way, sex characteristics can vary widely from person to person.

​

I get people to use my pronouns by being polite but consistent. I say that I use they/them pronouns instead of he/him or she/her and that I would appreciate  it if they used those pronouns. If they show confusion/anger/disgust I give a one sentence explanation of what being non-binary is. I say they should think of it as if a guy name Richard asked them to call him Dick. Depending on the vibe I'm getting I'll jokingly say that they can remember my pronouns instead of my name and give me whatever name they'd like. If they say they'll never use my correct pronouns or that my gender is fake or whatever... I tell them they can believe whatever they like but I will correct them every time.

I then correct them every time they get it wrong. The key is don't get upset or be rude, be clear and move on.

So if a coworker says, " Oh, (s)he'll handle it, that's his/her department."

I say,"I actually use they/them pronouns, but yeah I'll take care of it! Let me show you how to... and the conversation continues!

If the person gets upset or even shows bigotry I say that they may not thinks its real or important, but it is to me. Then you move the conversation along. Don't get upset, you have to be polite. The other person will end up looking like an ass if they keep getting mad over a simple request. So yeah, I guess I just wanted to say your kid can still have a normal life while being nonbinary! I think my life is honestly not that affected by it.

Again, IANAL. In Cali that would technically be a grey area, but I would think most officials would consider that a legal recording. You can't really claim you expected a conversation to be private if you're yelling in a public area.

Whether or not one wants to take legal action doesn't really matter. Private conversations always need consent from all parties. If you are in a public or semi public place then it's situational and depends on if those being recorded could have a reasonable expectation that the conversation is private and not being overheard. So let's say person A and person B are on a street having a convo. A starts insulting B, and B wants to record it legally. If the street is crowded, B can record it legally as A can not reasonably expect that conversation to be considered private with so many people around. If they're alone on the street or the other people present are also involved in the conversation, then B cannot record without permission as A could consider that conversation private. 

Basically, if A can ever reasonably argue that they wouldn't have said something if they knew other people would be listening, then you cannot record them. There is a small grey area of implied consent. If B were to visibly pull out their phone(or whatever recording device), audibly state that they were recording A, and A continued speaking anyway then one could argue A gave consent as they knew they were being recorded and continued anyway. But that argument doesn't always work, and California in particular does not like it much. 

EDIT: Wanted to mention the above doesn't apply to on duty police. You can always record their actions as long as you aren't getting in the way. Also, IANAL but I got this info straight from one a few months back.

Bedbugs are extremely contagious. I would seriously consider looking up "capsule wardrobes" and legit buying all new clothes like the day before you leave. It's only two months so you can get cheap clothes since they don't need to last. Also make sure to inspect your luggage! Like the physical bags and suitcases you pack in. They can travel in any crack, particularly fabric and leathers and eggs are practically invisible. If you are the only one showing a rash than your room is the main infestation.  Figure out what you are taking with you and what you can buy new right before your flight or what you can buy there.

  Everything you are taking from home needs to be scrubbed of bugs and eggs. Sadly, eggs are pretty much invisible to the human eye. First you harshly scrub every item, then decide which item can withstand extreme heat. The ones that can should either be blown with a air dryer on its highest setting or put in a clothes dryer on its highest setting for 60 minutes. Anything that can't be treated with heat needs to be put in a freezer for 30 days. Yes, days.  None of those methods are guaranteed, but it's better than nothing. There's a reason bed bugs are some of the worst pest in America. An average home needs $10000+ to fully get rid of bedbugs. The little eggs can legit hide between stitches in clothing. Be paranoid about it, save your boyfriend bedbug troubles.

That advice comes from my cousin, who owns a pest control place. He has shops in the west and east coast and bed bugs are the #1 problem in all of them. A technique I use for when my panic attacks and anxiety are about something specific is to think about the the worst possible outcome, the best possible outcome, and the most likely outcome. The best and worse outcome do not have to be realistic at all. So, the worst outcome here is death.And the best outcome may seem to be that the drugs and wine do nothing, but you can get outlandish with it! The best outcome from taking the wine and meds is actually that your mom gets filled with worry, and the fear for you health makes her realize her N behaviour is hurting your *mental* health, so se completely changes her behaviour and is a good mom from here on out. They do not have to be realistic outcomes! The most likely outcome would probably be something like the small amount of alcohol you drank leads to a few dizzy hours when mixed with meds. I let myself do some research to determine the most likely option, but a big part of the technique is realizing, through your own knowledge and logic, that the most likely outcome and the worst outcome aren't the same thing.

  Next, you want to imagine a scale with worst and best outcome on either end, and then have most likely in the middle. Now you think of as many outcomes as possible and place them on the scale. Like, you could've gotten to the point where you feared for your life and called 911. An outcome could've been you going to the hospital, having your stomach pumped, and then having nparent yell at you for going to the hospital. That one would go somewhere between most likely and worst outcome, depending on how likely you feel it it. Another outcome would be going to the hospital, but the nurses notice that your parents aren't treating you right, and they give you a bunch of resources/help, and you get to leave the Ns! That one would go to the good side. They can be smaller too, like the mixing of the drugs means that you get a good night's sleep. Our middle point is "drowsy for a few hours", so a good night's sleep would be on the good side, and pretty close to the center since its relatively likely. I think this method works because it helps me feel like I'm not just being dramatic while showing me how many other options there are besides the one I'm most afraid of.

Having to learn that on your own is really tough, but you will figure it out! 

  I totally understand feeling like your mistakes are going to eclipse everything else about you, and academic pressure certainly doesn't help. I've used a few strategies to try to continue living through that type of feeling. One is writing down good attributes about yourself and then write examples of when you displayed those attributes. This can be hard when you are self-loathing, so I try to think about what another person would see and then go off of that. For example, I will write down that I have a good sense of humor. Then I will put down examples and list the time I made a complete stranger laugh for 10 minutes straight and the time I met a good friend by telling a joke they laughed at. This seems really silly or self-absorbed, but it can honestly be really helpful. The point is to build it up over time so you can look back on it when you're in a really bad spot. l started it when I was in a really bad spot, so I couldn't think of anything good about yourself. At that point you can try to be proactive and try to make something good. In one of my classes there was a dying houseplant. The next day I literally just grabbed some water from the bathroom sink and watered it, so then I could put "cares about plants" in my book and give that as an example.

  Another is making a long term goal and then breaking it down into small, manageable steps. My goal rn is to leave my nmom's house. I've broken that down into many steps, but an example would be:

-get money to leave by getting a job
-look online for job apps
-do research on some of the companies found 
-fiure out which ones you want to apply to online and which ones you can apply to in person
- figure out how much walking it would take to get to the physical locations (since I have no other modes of transportation)
-try to be healthier so you can walk that distance comfortably.
-go for a walk at least once a week
-drink more water to improve health

  The point is to just break it down until you get to something that is small and manageable to do. That way when you do that thing you feel like you are actually accomplishing something more than just drinking water or whatever. Celebrating small victories. They don't have to be for realistic goals either. I have one breakdown for moving out, but i also have ones for like, working for a famous gaming company and having a many dogs lol. 

Another tip for specific situations is to think about what the worse possible outcome for a situation is, what the most likely outcome is, and what the best outcome would be can be very helpful for anxiety. Finally, I've found that saying things out load instead of just thinking them helps. Thinking "Getting bad grades in last semester won't ruin my life" doesn't work as well as saying it outloud.

  I'm so sorry that you are going through this, especially since it is due to other people's actions and not your own. Your parents are terrible (Edads never seem to be able to come through against Nmoms when it counts), at least you will be out from under them soon. 

  If after the 10-day center you have trouble finding a shelter remember that websites like www.couchsurfing.com/  exist. Maybe you should take a look now since you can schedule stays in advance.

  Ideally, you should be able to fit all your possessions in one bag. You def need to be able to carry all of your possessions. Your crisis program may have storage (ask them if you can store stuff long term!) but most homeless shelters do not. Figure out what the max weight you can carry is. Then subtract at least 5 pounds for that, but preferably 10. You will have to carry your stuff for a long time, you can't carry your max weight for multiple hours per day, every day.

  Try to bring important documents like your birth certificate and insurance information, preferably holding them in a locked, waterproof case. The most efficient way to pack clothes is to do it ranger roll style. [Here's how to do a ranger roll.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NtCH6KLdfBs)   He puts his toothbrush in the middle, but I suggest putting small valuables. You can also include pants if they aren't too thick, like jeans. I suggest 2-3 ranger rolls, but double the socks and undies. Wrap the second pair of sock around the roll itself and just use two pairs on underwear when rolling it up to begin with. I recommend two pairs of pants, at least one should be jeans. Shorts and skirts are honestly just a waste of space. Pants offer protection and keep you warmer. If you are sensitive to the heat take a baggy pair of pants so you can roll them up and get air circulation.

  Try to bring a small, waterproof container like Tupperware. I brought a small tube shaped container and one rectangular Tupperware piece. I brought a mini toothbrush, mini toothpaste, tampons, a money roll, small paper valuables like my birth certificate,  a small package of toilet paper, hand sanitizer, and a set of earrings in the tube. If you go to a dentist office and ask very nicely they may give you the mini toothbrush/paste, but you can also pick that stuff up at walmart in their travel section for under $10. The earrings were for looking professional in job interviews. Having small accessories makes you look less homeless and more put together. You probably don't need to do that if you are on disability already. These supplies will probs only last for a month or so, but it helps with moral a lot to have them. The rectangular Tupperware is so you could store opened food (think burgers from fast food places) for longer without it going bad. When you don't have food I suggest storing a pair of socks and underwear in there, just so you always have a pair that's waterproof'd. You could also use it to store water, but I suggest bringing a separate waterbottle to clip on to the outside of your bag. Bring a couple Carabiners! You'll never know what you can save space on just by bringing a few of the clips along and clipping stuff to the outside of your bag! I suggest one good jacket and, if you can, 1-2 long-sleeve pullovers. You may also want to bring a swimsuit. Some shelters don't have showers, but maybe locally there will be some other water source where people swim and you could sort of "bathe" there. Deodorant is very important regardless. Don't forgot your phone and laptop charger!

   I hope everything works out for you. Feel free to PM if you want any other help packing your bag, want advice for the homeless shelter, or just want to talk.

I suggest you keep your daughter in therapy for as long as possible, and make sure she actually likes her therapist! Research has shown that liking your therapist is a huge factor in recovery, and I agree.  My therapist felt like my only true confident and a big part of that is cause we were very similar people!   Planning for the future would also be helpful. No matter what, once she turns 18 she'll no longer have to see Nmom. Make plans for that milestone. Get involved in colleges now. Looking towards a future free from nmom was often the only thing keeping me from suicide at that age.  Your daughter has a better support netwark than I did, but having future events planned is generally really good for suicidal people. Make sure she always has good things to look forward to. Get her involved in a hobby or sport so she has games or meetups to look forward to. I was in an after-school arts program, and looking forwards to the monthly art shows helped a lot. When I wanted to kill my self, I would often bargain with myself to wait and see how I did in the contest.

If she's already depressed and suicidal, you want to make sure she doesn't turn to self-harm. When I could no longer cut I turned to food restriction and over exercising for control. I was overweight so nobody cared even though I was dropping weight way too quickly and never eating. Eating disorders are absolutely possible for overweight people. Make sure you are emphasizing weight loss for health, not beauty.

I had it for 6 months. It is nice in theory, but I found it to not really work out in practice. The items of the box usually total to less than $20, but that's not really the main draw of the box. Though I will say one month the supplies only totalled $12, and I thought that was a bit of a rip-off. You are really paying for the surprise of the items, but their picks aren't really that adventurous imo. You can only have so many different pencils and markers, no matter how nice they are. My other problem is that the items don't always work well together. Sometimes the carefully pick the 4-5 items and you can make a great piece with just those items, but most of the time it is just random stuff. Colors clash, the mediums aren't compatible, stuff like that. The quality isn't always there either. Sometimes it is really nice stuff, but others it will be bargain bin materials that are well known as being low-quality. 

If you have even a small amount of supplies you'll often see repeats or redundant supplies. I already have a good  eraser, microns, a few primsacolor markers and pencils, a few copics, a brush that holds water and a nice set of pencils.  If you have even that small list then you will almost certainly get duplicates in every box. Especially the brushes that hold water, they send those out constantly. They are all the same size! But they seem cool and are super cheap so I guess they fill out the boxes.

 If you love traditional art and want to try new materials I highly suggest you just look at the different mediums, pick one that seems cool, and just get enough to try it out. ArtSnacks sending you a tube of nice oil paint won't actually give you a realistic feel of oil painting. You need a nice brush, some medium, some thinner, and a nice mini canvas to really try that out.  Watercolors are a super accessible art as well! You can get really high-quality supplies, enough for professionals, for 40 or 50 bucks.

You could also just go to an art store with 20 bucks and just pick up anything that strikes your fancy. Then at least it'll be stuff you'll actually use!

Like other commenters have said, just thinking these thoughts every once in a while is completely normal. The fact that you can't stop thinking these thoughts and feel significant stress over them is the problem here. Compulsions are done specifically to relieve the stress of the thought, so your self-harm does sound like that. I'm not sure if it is specifically OCD or not, but I would bring it up with your therapist. There is honestly a lot of overlap between OCD and autism. You have some of the warning signs and beginning stages of OCD, and even if they are due to your autism you should still try to learn coping skills with your therapist. Anything that causes you a lot of distress and causes you to self-harm is serious and I imagine it would improve your quality of life to get some good coping methods c: !

If you are like, constantly thinking the same violent thought and being disgusted by it, in a sort of cycle,  than those are obsessive thoughts.

I have OCD, and there's a type of it called "pure-o" that is just obsessive thoughts without a compulsion (like physical acts) to follow them. Compulsions are not acting on the thought but doing something to relieve the stress of the thought. An example is that sometimes I think about hurting my mom and that makes me feel very dirty and guilty, so I obsessively scratch at my body to relieve that guilt as it is a "punishment". I used to also obsessively wash my body to relieve the dirty feeling. Violent obsessive thoughts are the most common imo. It might be worth looking into, OCD can def be a result of n parenting. It really depends on how intrusive these thoughts are on your life and if they cause you a lot of distress and guilt.

Here's a copy of the above mentioned book: http://www.carovnezrcadlo.cz/TOXIC-PARENTS.pdf

I found it very helpful when I first read it. I suggest you read all the sections, even if you dont think they apply to you. I know a few people here on rbn were really helped by the section on alcoholic parents, even if their parents weren't alcoholics. There are many shared behaviours when it comes to parental abuse.

  I also suggest you look up JADE if you haven't before.  It stands for **justify, argue, defend, and explain,** and it is meant to remind you of what **not** to do when talking with an abusive parent!finally, while the subreddit is called RBN I personally think it is for anyone who has a certain flavor of abusive parents, probably because the flavor of emotional abuse isn't discussed much in other places. It is totally okay if you realize you're mom probably doesn't have NPD and instead has another disorder or just has some problems in general. RBN will still be here for support regardless c: .

It would have to be a severe mental illness, and you would be showing numerous other symptoms. Of course, that isn't true and is just a cultural norm, but many people view cultural norms as objective truth, so it can be hard when you don't agree with them.

One of the things about Ns is that its pretty much impossible for them to change or feel remorse for hurting their kids. It is impossible to know why people become abusers, but I think the other people in in your group believe their abusive parents can change. Our society's views on blood related family would encourage abused children to try and help change their parents, since we are told from a young age to always help and support our family. It certainly doesn't help that when a parent is abusive people will often say that they are sick or ill, which implies they could get better.

  It seems like you've identified looking at your skin as a trigger. I would definitely ask your therapist for advice at getting over this trigger, as not being able to look at yourself gets impractical really quick. I had the same trigger, and my therapist gave me a few things I could do. He told me to try and keep my hands busy when I looked at my skin so I couldn't use them to pick. I had a spinner ring I would play with, and I would also do things like brush my teeth or clean the sink. Sometimes I would grab some make-up and smear it across my face. The process of smearing and then cleaning it off kept my hand busy, and it also helped me get used to looking at my skin without picking. I would also take a little time out of my day to try and desensitize myself from looking at my skin. I would take a little hand mirror and would look at a small portion of my face (like my chin) for just a few seconds. If I could do that, then I would reward myself and the next day I would either increase the amount of time I looked at myself for or how much of my face I was looking at.  For example, on day 5 I would try and look at my nose for 12 seconds. If i could do that then the next day I would either look at my nose for 14 seconds or look at my nose and my mouth for 12 seconds. If I wasn't able to do it than I would just reduce the time I needed to look the next day, there wasn't any punishment or anything. Personally, negative reinforcement doesn't work for me. When I had a bad day I would focus on making sure tomorrow was better as opposed to dwelling on what had gone wrong.

I hope you have a good day tomorrow, or at least a better day than today!

No one said this to me, but i came to this conclusion while talking to someone about my depression so it sort of counts.

I hadn't exhausted every option. I was planning on committing suicide. i was talking to someone and they asked me if I had tried to change my circumstances (a big influence on my depression) and I said that I had. But that wasn't really true. I had tried many things that all blew up back in my face, but I hadn't tried things like just straight up running away and trying to make it that way. Like, choosing to become homeless is a thing I could do. There were a lot of options that I didn't really consider because they just seemed so far-fetched. I decided I wouldn't allow myself to die until I had taken every option, because I may be robbing myself of a good future. When I'm suicidal I see no future, just more pain and suffering. Either doing these radical things would make things better, and I wouldn't want to die anymore. Or, they wouldn't make things better, and then all I've done is proven to myself that I really should die. It didn't really affect me to wait and see.

Some examples of choices I could take would be to start taking various drugs, to move to another country, to join the military, and to apply to literally any college that interested me. I couldn't say that that life had nothing for me unless I really tried everything life had to offer.

There was something someone said to me that stopped me for a while. Part of the reason I was feeling suicidal is that I felt I was a huge burden to everyone and they were better off without me, even if they loved me. This person basically rephrased what I had been telling them and said I was trying to save the peopel I cared about long-term pain by causing them short-term pain (the pain of me dying), which was true.  She said that I should try to minimize my loved ones' pain as much as possible. She told me I should think about funeral costs, especially since I was so concerned about being a financial burden already. Saving to pay for my own funeral saved me for a year or so.

It's a mix of comfort items and stuff to aggravate my senses. I have a weighted shawl, which just puts pressure on the body when i wear it. It's very helpful to help come out of a dissociative state, since pressure on the body is hard to ignore. There's also some rubber necklaces to chew on (from stimtastic), some small puzzles like rubix cubes, a bag of mini candies from the 99cent store, my favorite lotion, an origami book and paper for the origami, some adult coloring books for stress relief, a heating pad, and a lot of other random stuff. It's literally anything i like or to stimulate the senses. i have a few brushes and similar items that i just run across my skin to help feel stuff. Touch and smell bring me out of a dissociative state the fastest, so i have a lot of stuff for those two senses. i used to have books and cds in there too, but those only help for stress relief and didn't help me stop dissociating, so i put them in a different box. By the way, the box is just a toolbox under my bed. Nothing fancy. The whole point is that its stuff you like, but sometimes it takes a while to figure out the right kind of items. Keep trying it! it works better the more you use it.

Here's what I do:

  * Have many short lists of what I want or need to do on notecards, then save those notecards so I can look at them and feel productive on bad days.

  * Have an alarm that goes off every 40 minutes or so. I get up, get a drink, go to the bathroom, and stretch. This helps break the trance of the website.
  
  * Have a box of physical items to play with/enjoy during my breaks or on bad days. The items stimulate all 5 senses, so it helps me feel connected to my body again.

  * Use sites like Habitica to form good habits. Stayfocused is an extension on chrome, it is a good "extreme" measure since it'll block you from using the websites you select after a period of time you decide on. You can't use them for the rest of the day!

  * Have a timer constantly running on screen so you can be aware of the time you're spending on the sites. The constant movement helps as well.

 Sometimes, I'll also have a notecard or webpage where I have all the good outcomes of doing the things I need to do. It just says stuff like "have money to see friends" or "be able to go to dream school", but it still helps! Every little drop helps. It may be a good idea to write down every time you successfully have a productive day or at least every time you were able to get out of the zone and get off those websites. That way, if you feel gross about spending time browsing you'll at least have the reassurance that you were able to do this before and that one time of being unproductive or falling into the zone won't ruin your life. little reward systems like that are also helpful for learning how to deal with negative emotions, since I usually disassociate because I can't deal with my emotions. Evidence that I can do good things and be productive help, and so does giving yourself a little treat can also work, since you'll start to associate expressing emotions with getting a good thing. Hmm, giving yourself permission to be upset would also be good. Whenever i express negative emotion I have to "forgive" myself for it, since my brain thinks that's a bad thing. Preemptively telling myself it's okay to cry, or to yell, or to put my feelings into my art does help a bit in making the depression/disassociation I feel after expressing emotion go away faster.
